title: Regression in 2.4.2: sdist install fails as root on Python < 3.10.12 / < 3.11.4 with TypeError: getgrnam() argument 'name' must be str, not None
body:
Since 2.4.2, `poetry install` fails as root while extracting an sdist on Pythons whose `tarfile` has no `data_filter`. We hit it in a Docker build on `python:3.10.4-bullseye` with `crontab 1.0.4`, `facepy 1.0.12` and `PyMeeus 0.5.12`, which have no wheel on PyPI.

On these Pythons `extractall()` in `poetry/utils/helpers.py` uses the ported CPython 3.14 data filter added in #11027. The filter sets `uid`, `gid`, `uname` and `gname` to `None`, and members are then extracted with `archive.extract(member, dest, set_attrs=not member.isdir())`. As root, `tarfile._extract_member()` calls `chown()`, where these Python versions have no `None` guard:

```python
# CPython 3.10.11, tarfile.py
try:
    if grp:
        g = grp.getgrnam(tarinfo.gname)[2]
except KeyError:
    pass
```

`grp.getgrnam(None)` raises `TypeError`, which is not caught, and the install aborts. CPython has `if grp and tarinfo.gname:` there from 3.10.12 and 3.11.4 on.

Checked with the same command, `poetry install --no-root` of `crontab==1.0.4` as root:

| Python | poetry 2.4.2 | poetry 2.4.1 |
|---|---|---|
| 3.10.4 | fails | ok |
| 3.10.11 | fails | not checked |
| 3.10.12 | ok | not checked |
| 3.11.3 | fails | not checked |
| 3.11.4 | ok | not checked |
| 3.10.18 | ok | not checked |

In 2.4.1 the same fallback branch validated member paths only and did not change ownership attributes.

```console
$ docker run --rm -u root python:3.10.4-bullseye bash -c '
  pip install -q "poetry==2.4.2"
  mkdir /t && cd /t
  printf "[project]\nname=\"repro\"\nversion=\"0.1.0\"\nrequires-python=\">=3.10\"\ndependencies=[\"crontab==1.0.4\"]\n" > pyproject.toml
  POETRY_VIRTUALENVS_CREATE=false poetry install --no-root'
```

The same command with `poetry==2.4.1` succeeds.

- Run the install as a non-root user, verified on `python:3.10.4-bullseye` with 2.4.2.
- Use Python 3.10.12+ or 3.11.4+, verified above.
- Pin `poetry==2.4.1`.

**Poetry Installation Method:** pip

**Operating System:** Debian 11 (`python:3.10.4-bullseye` container), also seen on GitHub Actions `ubuntu-24.04`

**Poetry Version:** 2.4.2

```
cache-dir = "/root/.cache/pypoetry"
installer.max-workers = null
installer.no-binary = null
installer.only-binary = null
installer.parallel = true
installer.re-resolve = false
solver.lazy-wheel = true
virtualenvs.create = false
```

<details><summary>poetry-runtime.log</summary>

```
5  poetry/installation/chef.py:60 in prepare
     →  60│         return self._prepare_sdist(
4  poetry/installation/chef.py:106 in _prepare_sdist
     → 106│             extractall(source=archive, dest=archive_dir, zip=zip)
3  poetry/utils/helpers.py:529 in extractall
     → 529│                     archive.extract(member, dest, set_attrs=not member.isdir())
2  /usr/local/lib/python3.10/tarfile.py:2090 in extract
     → 2090│             self._extract_member(tarinfo, os.path.join(path, tarinfo.name),
1  /usr/local/lib/python3.10/tarfile.py:2178 in _extract_member
     → 2178│             self.chown(tarinfo, targetpath, numeric_owner)

TypeError
getgrnam() argument 'name' must be str, not None
at /usr/local/lib/python3.10/tarfile.py:2284 in chown
    2283│                     if grp:
  → 2284│                         g = grp.getgrnam(tarinfo.gname)[2]
Cannot install crontab.

title: Docs preview will fail for labeled fork PRs since the actions/checkout 7.0.1 update
body:
Since #11071 (2026-09-19), `docs.yaml` pins `actions/checkout` 7.0.1. Since 2026-07-20, `actions/checkout` refuses to check out a fork pull request's code in a `pull_request_target` workflow unless the step sets `allow-unsafe-pr-checkout: true` ([changelog](https://github.blog/changelog/2026-06-18-safer-pull_request_target-defaults-for-github-actions-checkout/)). Before the update, 6.0.2 predated that change.

So the second checkout in the `deploy` job (`ref: ${{ github.event.pull_request.head.sha }}`, sparse `docs`) will fail the next time a fork PR gets the `impact/docs` label. The last fork preview that worked was https://github.com/python-poetry/poetry/actions/runs/35355542954 (2026-09-18, on 6.0.2); fork runs since then were skipped, so nothing has failed yet.

Docs PRs from forks would get no preview once labeled. Separately, from 2026-11-02 GitHub blocks `pull_request_target` by default on public repositories without an Actions policy allowing it ([changelog](https://github.blog/changelog/2026-09-17-workflow-execution-protections-in-github-actions-generally-available/)), so the preview would also need that policy.

Since the step checks out only `docs` and the content is built as data by the website repo's code, `allow-unsafe-pr-checkout: true` on that one step may be what you want here. That's your call. Another option is to build on `pull_request` and deploy from a `workflow_run` workflow.

_Found with prt-check (https://github.com/UniteAndCreateForLife/prt-check). Drafted with AI assistance (Claude); the facts and links were checked against their sources before posting._
label: BUG

import pandas as pd

2    False
dtype: boolean

Docs should reflect that `fill_value` accepts a string value when

To:

title: Installation guide uses outdated "source activate" conda syntax
body:
https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/getting_started/install.html#installing-with-conda

The Installation guide instructs users to activate a conda environment using legacy syntax:
```
# On Linux or MacOS
source activate name_of_my_env
# On Windows
activate name_of_my_env

`source activate` / `activate` was conda's activation syntax before conda 4.4 (released in 2017), and has since been replaced by `conda activate` which works across all operating systems (e.g. Windows, MacOS, Linux). 

Moreover, the "[Creating a development environment](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/development/contributing_environment.html#option-1-using-conda-recommended)" guide in the pandas documentation already uses `conda activate pandas-dev` as its primary instruction. Replace the  `source activate` / `activate` instructions with the single modern command:

conda activate name_of_my_env
```

title: "10 minutes to pandas" guide doesn't explain that double brackets return a DataFrame, not a Series

https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/user_guide/10min.html#getitem

The "Getitem ([])" section of the "10 minutes to pandas" tutorial shows that a single label in brackets will return a Series:
```
df["A"]
```
It also shows that a list of multiple labels returns a DataFrame:
```
df[["B", "A"]]
```

It never shows the specific case of a list containing a single label (e.g. `df[["A"]]`, which also returns a DataFrame). However, since `df["A"]` and `df[["A"]]` look nearly identical but return different object types, this could be a common point of confusion for beginners, yet isn't directly illustrated anywhere on this page. The distinction is already covered in the more comprehensive "[Indexing and selecting data](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/user_guide/indexing.html#basics)" guide, but it is not mentioned in the "10 minutes to pandas" tutorial, where many new users will actually first encounter column selection.

Add a short note and example directly after the existing `df[["B", "A"]]` example, describing `df[["A"]]` and stating that it returns a DataFrame containing that one column, rather than a Series.

title: Notes of `pd.crosstab` contradicts Examples on Categorical handling
body:
https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/reference/api/pandas.crosstab.html#pandas.crosstab

The Notes section of `crosstab` states unconditionally that all categories
of Categorical input are included. Since the default is `dropna=True`,
unobserved categories are in fact excluded, and the Examples section of the
same docstring already says so explicitly.

Current Notes paragraph, which also appears in `crosstab` function in `pandas.core.reshape.pivot`
```
Any input passed containing Categorical data will have **all** of its categories included in the cross-tabulation, even if the actual data does not contain any instances of a particular category.

```python
>>> foo = pd.Categorical(["a", "b"], categories=["a", "b", "c"])
>>> bar = pd.Categorical(["d", "e"], categories=["d", "e", "f"])
>>> pd.crosstab(foo, bar)
col_0  d  e
row_0
a      1  0
b      0  1
>>> pd.crosstab(foo, bar, dropna=False)
col_0  d  e  f
row_0
a      1  0  0
b      0  1  0
c      0  0  0
```

I Suggest to change the Notes like below:
```
categories included in the cross-tabulation when `dropna=False`, even if the actual data does not contain any instances of a particular category. With the default `dropna=True`, categories with no observations are excluded.
```

title: `poetry build` misses package in a path excluded by .gitignore
body:
I built a project whose python files are located in "src/main/python/myproject" using `poetry build` with this pyproject.toml:

```
[build-system]
requires = [ "poetry-core>=2.0.0",]
build-backend = "poetry.core.masonry.api"

...

[tool.poetry]
packages = [{include = "myproject", from = "src/main/python"}]
```

The **python files in the "myproject" folder** are created by protobuf, are thus not part of the project source code and therefore **excluded from version control by ".gitignore".**
The resulting sdist and wheel files do not contain the source code in the "myproject" package.

I'd expect that if a package is explicitly mentioned in the pyproject.toml to be an included package, its content should not be ignored by poetry, even if listed in the .gitignore file.
This behaviour is new in poetry 2.x.

Either do not add files relevant for the build to ".gitignore", or use `include` config rather than `packages`.

title: pre-commit-update instead of no auto-update at all
body:
As per [this issue](https://github.com/python-poetry/poetry/issues/9312) and [docs](https://python-poetry.org/docs/pre-commit-hooks/#why-does-pre-commit-autoupdate-not-update-to-the-latest-version), it is obvious that we can't use `pre-commit autoupdate` feature with poetry - but that means manual update every time we want the newest (stable) version of the repo.

As per description, the impact is very clear - pre-commit config that is not manually updated/revisited will get outdated sooner or later...

I came across a [blog post](https://blog.nathanv.me/posts/python-tooling-vol-2) that mentioned this with an alternative solution:

> You may notice, I’m also using the third party [pre-commit-update](https://pypi.org/project/pre-commit-update/) tool, since I find it works better than the built in pre-commit autoupdate command. [Poetry](https://python-poetry.org/docs/pre-commit-hooks/#why-does-pre-commit-autoupdate-not-update-to-the-latest-version) in particular conflicts with this built-in command.

So I checked out `pre-commit-update` and it works perfectly for our use case. It is very configurable and you can even use it as a pre-commit hook itself.

Minimal example would be:
```
repos:
-   repo: https://gitlab.com/vojko.pribudic.foss/pre-commit-update
    rev: v0.5.1post1
    hooks:
    -   id: pre-commit-update
-   repo: https://github.com/python-poetry/poetry
    rev: 1.8.0  # add version here
    hooks:
    -   id: poetry-check
    -   id: poetry-lock
    -   id: poetry-export
    -   id: poetry-install
```
    
Which - on commit - would produce:

```
✘ poetry - 1.8.0 -> 1.8.3
Changes detected and applied
```

You can even do all sorts of other things - such as excluding the repo, pin it to a certain tag, use unstable versions - etc.

So my proposal would be to perhaps offer that as an alternative in the docs :)

[tool.poetry.urls]

```

I was able to fix this by using capital keys instead. This works for both poetry commands _and_ pip commands:
```toml
[tool.poetry.urls]
Repository = "xyz"
```

Should the docs be updated to use capital keys or should the source code be updated like so?:
```python
if name == "repository" and url == package.urls["repository"]:
    continue
if name == "documentation" and url == package.urls["documentation"]:
    continue
```

title: Data Entropy & Information Loss Tracking for DataFrame Transformations
body:
Pandas does not provide any method to measure the information loss which occurs when DataFrame transformations are applied. 

Data resolution decreases permanently through common operations because users cannot observe this reduction which results from rounding and binning and aggregation and encoding and filtering and deduplication. Users create data compression that exceeds proper limits which leads to the loss of valuable information without their awareness. 

I want pandas to provide users with information loss measurements which show how transformations affect data processing because this will help them choose preprocessing methods and identify excessive operations which will improve their data pipeline trust.

The system will start tracking operational data transformations through its mandatory tracking system which will record every DataFrame transformation that occurs. 

The feature would:

- The system will calculate entropy values at the column level using Shannon entropy for discrete data and histogram-based entropy for continuous data.

- The system will measure information loss through its normalized entropy difference calculation which compares two different states.

- The system will track information loss from operations that occur within a monitoring environment.

Example API:
       with df.track_information() as info:
           df["price"] = df["price"].round(0)
           df["age_group"] = pd.cut(df["age"], bins=5)

        info.report()

Conceptual implementation

      def entropy(series):
          if is_discrete(series):
              p = value_counts(series) / len(series)
              return -sum(p * log2(p))
          else:
               bins = adaptive_bins(series)
               p = histogram(series, bins) / len(series)
               return -sum(p * log2(p))

The system performs lazy entropy calculations which apply to specific columns that undergo changes. The system applies adaptive binning to continuous data in order to produce consistent estimation results. The system calculates dataset-level information loss by summing all column-specific information losses. The feature requires user activation because it creates no performance impact until the user decides to use it. The system enables users to monitor DataFrame transformation impacts on information content while maintaining the original pandas functional behavior.

Multiple different methods exist as potential alternatives for evaluation. 

Relying on documentation or user discipline Users would need to decide how much information they lost through their transformation work. The current system proves unmanageable because it creates errors while users cannot track the total impact which develops throughout their different workflows.

Heuristic warnings for specific operations Pandas should develop a system which generates alerts about dangerous functions which include binning and rounding as destructive actions. The system would operate at a broad level but its results would not show the actual information loss degree which occurs through a specific dataset.

Downstream model metrics (e.g., feature importance, performance) The model behavior permits users to infer information loss yet this method only works during the machine learning stage and it does not serve general data analysis or reporting purposes.

External profiling or data quality tools Existing tools examine missing data and data distribution patterns and schema validation processes, but they lack the ability to monitor how data transformations create information loss which they can trace back to particular processes.

The available alternatives failed to meet requirements because they lacked the ability to show information loss which occurs during pandas operations at both direct and transformation-level contexts.

title: Allow `np.ndarray` in `check_result_array` for certain `dtype`
body:
Aggregations are using `check_result_array` to verify that the aggregation operation reduced the dimension. To do so it checks that the given `obj` is not a `np.ndarray` and if so the expected `dtype` is at least `object`. The expected `dtype` hereby is the `dtype` of the `group` before the aggregation. This can be an issue if the actual aggregated `obj` is expected to still be an `np.ndarray` but the expected `dtype` is not `object`.

`_aggregate_series_pure_python` calls `check_result_array(res, group.dtype)` to verify result of aggregation:
https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/blob/433b140936aadec0f42c46e4e827f6f545569bbc/pandas/core/groupby/ops.py#L986-L1005

`check_result_array`:
https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/blob/433b140936aadec0f42c46e4e827f6f545569bbc/pandas/core/groupby/ops.py#L81-L89

The `dtype` parameter in `check_result_array` lets us know what the `dtype` of the `group` was. As far as I know every `dtype` has the `type` property that specifies of which type a singular element of an `array` with this `dtype` would be. Consider the following example:
```python
>>> df = pd.DataFrame({"A": [1,1,2], "B": [10,20,30]})
>>> df
   A   B
0  1  10
1  1  20
2  2  30
>>> df.dtypes
A    int64
B    int64
dtype: object
>>> grouped = df.groupby("A").agg("first")
>>> grouped
    B
A
1  10
2  30
>>> grouped.dtypes
B    int64
dtype: object
>>> grouped["B"].dtype
dtype('int64')
>>> type(grouped["B"].iloc[0]) == df["B"].dtype.type
True
```
The `type` of an element of the aggregation result (here "`first"` function) is the same as the `dtype.type` of the original column `df["B"]`.

In my opinion the same should be true for other `dtypes`. Therefore if this `dtype.type` is an `np.ndarray` then `check_result_array` should not raise a `ValueError` as it is likely that the aggregation still worked as expected.

Such a check could be implemented with:
```python
isinstance(obj, dtype.type)
```

Or in the full function (description still would have to be updated to accommodate the change):
```python
 def check_result_array(obj, dtype) -> None: 
     # Our operation is supposed to be an aggregation/reduction. If 
     #  it returns an ndarray, this likely means an invalid operation has 
     #  been passed. See test_apply_without_aggregation, test_agg_must_agg 
     if isinstance(obj, np.ndarray): 
         if dtype != object or isinstance(obj, dtype.type): 
             # If it is object dtype, the function can be a reduction/aggregation 
             #  and still return an ndarray e.g. test_agg_over_numpy_arrays 
             raise ValueError("Must produce aggregated value") 
```

Not sure if there are alternative solutions.

I stumbled on the issue during my tests, specifically `BaseGroupbyTests::test_groupby_agg_extension` which calls `first` as the aggregation function, of the Astropy ExtensionArray that I am currently writing. Its main feature is the support of Astropy `Quantity` objects that support physical units and are themselve a subclass of `np.ndarray`. Therefore `check_result_array` fails as the result of an aggregation can be a `zerodim` `Quantity` object, which is not scalar but still a `np.ndarray`

All other issues I found about `check_result_array` seem to be related to `pd.Series.mode` as this aggregation can also create arrays as a result if there are more than one mode:
- https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/issues/38534
- https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/issues/41368
- https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/issues/44119
label: FEATURE

title: Suggestion: link a RAG / LLM debugging checklist (WFGY Problem Map) in the docs
body:
Hi pandas team,

thank you for maintaining such a foundational library. pandas is often the first stop for people who are building data workflows that later feed into LLM or RAG systems (corpus cleaning, chunking, metadata enrichment, offline evaluation, and so on).

I maintain an MIT-licensed project called **WFGY Problem Map**, which is a 16-question diagnostic checklist for RAG / LLM pipelines in production. It focuses on data and retrieval failure modes (ingestion gaps, chunking pathologies, vector store issues, evaluation leaks, etc), not on model weights.

Why I think this might be relevant for pandas users:
- Many real-world RAG systems start from pandas DataFrames (documents, logs, event streams) before anything is embedded or indexed.
- Several of the 16 failure modes are about how tabular and semi-structured data are transformed and filtered before they reach a retriever.
- The checklist is tooling-agnostic and can be applied no matter whether people use pandas alone or in combination with other frameworks.

For credibility: the same checklist has already been included in a few curated / academic ecosystems such as
- ToolUniverse by Harvard MIMS Lab  
- Multimodal RAG Survey by QCRI LLM Lab  
- Rankify (University of Innsbruck)

Suggestion:

If you think it could be useful for your users, would you consider adding a small link in your docs or resource section such as

> “RAG / LLM debugging checklist: WFGY Problem Map (16 failure modes)”  
> https://github.com/onestardao/WFGY/blob/main/ProblemMap/README.md

Project home: https://github.com/onestardao/WFGY

Thanks again for all your work on pandas and for considering this small suggestion.

Best,  
PSBigBig

title: Utilize `_values_for_json` in `Series.to_json`
body:
ExtensionArrays can define a `_values_for_json` method if the standard numpy array with `object` dtype returned by `__array__` is not serializable because the objects themselves are not serializable. However this method is only utilized for `DataFrame.to_json` trough `BlockManager.column_arrays`:

https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/blob/353763e607745e6fad90fed89efe97bd1f87ebae/pandas/core/internals/managers.py#L1249-L1251

In `Series.to_json` no path leads to the `_values_for_json` method and nearly always `__array__` is utilized. Therefore some ExtensionArrays are only JSON serializable if they are in a `DataFrame` and not a `Series`, which in my opinion also could be considered a bug.

In short modify the `objToJSON.c` file to also call `_values_for_json` for pandas `Series`.

With the help of GitHub Copilot I was able to trace the issue to the `get_values` function, specifically the following lines:
https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/blob/353763e607745e6fad90fed89efe97bd1f87ebae/pandas/_libs/src/vendored/ujson/python/objToJSON.c#L201-L213

- In `201` we are effectively calling `Series.values` and assign it to `values`.
- If the `Series` and therefore `values` is not empty `values` now is a numpy array or ExtensionArray.
- Next in `205` it is checked if `values` has a `__array__` attribute and if so calls it, that is also the path mentioned above that leads potentially to the numpy array of object dtype with not serializable objects in it.
- At last in `210` if none of the checks above worked it is checked if `values` is already a `np.ndarray` (and only that, so no subclass) and if not dereferences `values` and tries to create the array somewhere up the stack (if I understand it correctly).

My proposal would be to add another check after the empty check but before the `__array__` check. Similar to the `__array__` check it could test if `values` has a `_values_for_json` attribute (and therefore is an ExtensionArray) and if so calls that method to create the serializable numpy array. This check could work like the following snippet, but I have not tried it out yet. It would be important to include it before the `__array__` check as ExtensionArrays have that attribute too:
```c
else if (PyObject_HasAttrString(values, "_values_for_json")) {
    // We have gotten an ExtensionArray
    PyObject *array_values = PyObject_CallMethod(values, "_values_for_json", NULL);
    Py_DECREF(values);
    values = array_values;
}
```
Disclaimer: This snipped was developed with GitHub Copilot after chatting with it to understand how the `get_values` function works and asking if a check similar to `__array__` would also work in the designated spot. It also suggested to not make it an `else if` block but an `if` block so that if the return value of `_values_for_json` itself is not already a `np.ndarray` but an array-like object the following checks could still convert that object using the `__array__` attribute. In my opinion that is not necessary because the function signature of `_values_for_json` already specifies that the return value shall be a `np.ndarray` and the base implementation just calls `np.asarray(self)` which should also dispatch to `__array__`. I therefore modified the snipped above accordingly. As there currently do not seem to be any test for `_values_for_json`, adding tests that make sure that this method actually returns an `np.ndarray` and that the values inside are serializable seems sensible.

Always convert your `Series` to `DataFrame` with `sr.to_frame()` before JSON serialization, then the `_values_for_json` method of the ExtensionArray is already used.

I found this issue during my work for an external ExtensionArray to support astropy `Quantity` objects which are subclasses of `np.ndarray` but themselves not JSON serializable.

I also looked a bit around through the open issues regarding `Series` and JSON serialization and found #55426 by @jbrockmendel, there he wrote down some general notes about formatting of Ext

title: Add DataFrame.memory_report() for actionable dtype optimization suggestions
body: DataFrame.memory_usage() tells you how much memory a DataFrame uses, but gives no guidance on why or what to do about it. Users who want to optimize memory must: - Manually inspect each column's dtype - Know the integer/float downcast rules by heart - Manually check cardinality for object columns - Write their own loops to apply changes This is a very common pain point — especially for data engineers and analysts working with medium-to-large datasets who hit memory pressure and have no built-in tool to diagnose it. A new method DataFrame.memory_report() that: 1. Analyzes every column's current dtype and actual value range 2. Suggests the smallest safe dtype for each column 3. Explains why each suggestion is safe (value range, cardinality ratio) 4. Returns a rich MemoryReport object that is both human-readable and 5. machine-readable 6. Never modifies the DataFrame — purely diagnostic, zero side effects def memory_report( self, verbose: bool = True, category_threshold: float = 0.5, check_datetimes: bool = True, ) -> MemoryReport: """ Analyze memory usage and suggest safe dtype optimizations. Parameters ---------- verbose : bool, default True If True, print the full report to stdout. category_threshold : float, default 0.5 Suggest ``category`` dtype when unique ratio is below this value. For example, 0.5 means fewer than 50% unique values → suggest category. check_datetimes : bool, default True Attempt to detect datetime-parseable strings in object columns. Samples up to 200 rows to avoid scanning very large columns. Returns ------- MemoryReport Structured report with per-column diagnostics. Supports: - ``report.to_dataframe()`` — machine-readable table - ``report.apply(df)`` — apply all suggestions, returns new df - ``report.actionable`` — list of columns with suggestions - ``report.high_impact`` — columns with >= 50% savings potential """ df.info(memory_usage='deep'). This is the closest native.But no guidance on how to fix it. Design Decisions Zero side effects. memory_report() never modifies the DataFrame. Applying suggestions is always an explicit opt-in via report.apply(df). Safe-only suggestions. Every suggestion is lossless by default: Integer downcasts are validated against actual min/max values Float32 suggestions are validated: values are cast to float32 and checked for overflow before recommending apply() wraps each conversion in a try/except and warns on failure — it never raises Null awareness. The report flags columns with nulls so users know before applying dtype changes that may affect null representation. Overflow guard for floats. The implementation detects when a finite float64 value would become ±inf after float32 cast, and keeps float64. Composable return type. Returning a MemoryReport rather than just printing means the output is usable in notebooks, CI pipelines, and data quality checks.
label: FEATURE

title: Simplify reading vertically stacked CSV tables
body:
The overall goal is reading vertically stacked CSV files, with multiple tables.
There is no difficulty in writing such a file with pandas (just append) or reading and splitting horizontally stacked CSV files (but they can be inefficient and more complicated to write).
This is not technically a CSV format (according to RFC 4180, since column sizes differ) but a very slight generalisation of it.
It doesn't really have a name, but has been re-invented several times, with different ways of determining where to split the table.

I think the only form that really needs supporting are known specified lines, e.g. [[''], ['Col1', 'Col2']] would split on blank rows but also on Col1,Col2 rows. I had considered "when the number of columns changes", but I think that's a strictly less useful format (you can't have multiple tables with the same number of columns consecutively), and it could be extended in later if wanted.

Possible solutions I can think of (any one of the following):
   
   This would require the ability to reset the columns state of the reader (either by the user or as part of the implementation).
   If that is easy to do, then this might be the most straightforward way of implementing this feature.

   The simplest way of doing this is adding an option chunk_on = None, which can be set to a list of row values (permitted to include the blank row).
   Importantly the presence of this does not just cause the chunks to be broken off but also the number, header, names and types of columns to be reset (if not specified as a parameter) as if reading a new file. (But it does not reset if chunking because of chunksize, so the two are compatible.)

   If skip_blank_lines is True, then blank lines can end (if [''] is in chunk_on) but not begin or contribute to a chunk.
   I.e. consecutive skipped blank lines do not lead to 1x1 NA chunks, do not lead to 1x1 NAs before EOF or before other chunk_on rows, and do not lead to 1xN NA rows in previous or following chunks.
 

   If skip_blank_lines is False, then a blank line is interpreted as a row [''] and behaves the same as any other row (perhaps aside from NA conversion).
   If skip_blank_lines is True and [''] is not in chunk_on, then it is as if reading the file without blank lines in.
   (This should be the same as currently, aside from the new parameter cases.)

   Usage would look something like this
   ```CSV
   X,Y
   1,2
   3,4
   A,B,C
   x,y,3
   u,v,2
   ```

   abc = ['A', 'B', 'C']
   tables = {}

       # If it doesn't then this can be simpler, not saying that it should though.

       stored = tables.setdefault(key, chunk)

   1  3  4

   >>> tables[abc]
      A  B  C # str, str, int
   0  x  y  3
   1  u  v  2
   ```

   This is the simplest and fastest from the user's perspective but possibly the least convenient to implement, and raises many questions about the interface. This could return an iterable (forward compatible if changed to some object type) of the distinct tables.

title: Support %N directive in strptime parsing (to_datetime / Timestamp with format=)
body:
GH-29461 / PR GH-64899 added a `%N` directive to `Timestamp.strftime` and the
array-level `strftime`, formatting nanoseconds as a 9-digit zero-padded number.
The parsing side does not accept it, so `%N` output doesn't round-trip with the
same format string:

```python
>>> ts = pd.Timestamp("2020-03-14 15:32:52.192548651")
>>> fmt = "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S.%N"
>>> pd.to_datetime(ts.strftime(fmt), format=fmt)
ValueError: 'N' is a bad directive in format '%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S.%N'
```

Note that pandas' strptime already parses nanoseconds via `%f` (it accepts 1-9
digits, an extension over the stdlib's 6), so this is about symmetry and
round-tripping rather than new capability. Suggested in
https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/pull/64899#pullrequestreview-4481273478.

Accept `%N` in `format=` for `to_datetime`, `Timestamp`, and related parsing
paths, matching exactly 9 digits (vs `%f`'s 1-9). Likely just an entry next to
`"f"` in the `TimeRE` class and corresponding handling in `strptime.pyx`.

Keep parsing via `%f`, which already handles 9 digits — but then a format
string built for `%N` output can't be reused for parsing.

`Period.strftime` has long supported `%n`/`%N` for formatting only; linux
`date` uses `%N` for nanoseconds.

title: Support `tz_convert` on naive timestamps when naive tz specified
body:
It is quite common to defensively convert-or-assume timestamps to UTC, which means writing something like this:

```python
def my_function(df: pd.Dataframe, time: pd.Timestamp) -> pd.Dataframe:
    if time.tzinfo is None:
        time = time.tz_localize("UTC")
    else:
        time = time.tz_convert("UTC")
    ...
    return df.assign(time=time)
```

Alternatively an inline if can be used

```python
time = time.tz_localize("UTC") if time.tz is None else time.tz_convert("UTC")
```

But this is slightly longwinded, so often helper functions are repeated in loads of modules

```python
def _ensure_utc(time: pd.Timestamp) -> pd.Timestamp:
    return (
        time.tz_localize("UTC")
        if time.tz is None
        else time.tz_convert("UTC")
    )
```

My opinion is that neither the rather long if..else expression nor the usually-not-consistently-named helper method are very readable. There can also be challenges around proper typing on the helper method, when support for e.g. series and datetime index is required as well. This feature request is essentially asking for a shorthand that is native to Pandas for this pattern.

Add a keyword argument to `tz_convert` which specifies how naive timestamps should be interpreted, instead of raising an error:

```python
time = time.tz_convert("UTC", naive_tz="UTC")
```

It would be functionally equivalent to `time.tz_localize("UTC") if time.tz is None else time.tz_convert("UTC")` - just a shorthand. Of course, `tz_convert` on series, datetime index etc should have the same support.

"Keeping the status quo" is more verbose and works. The feature request is mainly to make the convert-or-assume pattern easier to both write and read.

But some alternatives that go along the same lines:

- Different keyword arg names, e.g. `.tz_convert("UTC", assume_naive="UTC")`
    - Particularly, putting the verb "assume" might be good for clarity of what the arg does. It's just longer so I didn't put it in the main suggestion (I think the main suggestion is clear enough).
- "Policy style" instead of specific tz, `.tz_convert("UTC", naive="assume_utc")`, `.tz_convert("UTC", naive="assume_local")`
    - This could have a default of `naive="raise"` which neatly describes the current behaviour correctly while keeping `tz=None` semantics constant. However it obviously loses the ability to set an arbitrary naive timezone to use. 
- Different specific method, e.g. `.tz_ensure("UTC", assume="UTC")`
    - If someone thinks we're changing the semantics of `tz_convert` too hard. I don't think so, but had to be mentioned.

title: UnicodeDecodeError from read_csv could suggest common alternative encodings
body:
I wish read_csv's UnicodeDecodeError gave me a hint about what to try next, instead of just failing with no direction.

When read_csv hits a UnicodeDecodeError (e.g. a Windows Excel export saved as cp1252), the error gives no indication that trying a different encoding is the likely fix.

Reproducible example (pandas 3.0.2):

with open('test.csv', 'wb') as f:
    f.write(b'name,note\n')
    f.write(b'test,em' + bytes([0x97]) + b'dash\n')  # valid cp1252, invalid utf-8

import pandas as pd
pd.read_csv('test.csv')

Result:
UnicodeDecodeError: 'utf-8' codec can't decode byte 0x97 in position 17: invalid start byte

This is a very common situation, Windows Excel commonly exports CSVs as cp1252, not utf-8, and the fix is almost always trying encoding='latin-1' or encoding='cp1252'. But nothing in the error message points there, so new users often don't realize encoding is even the problem.

Append a short hint to the UnicodeDecodeError raised during CSV parsing when the default utf-8 encoding fails and the user hasn't explicitly set encoding.

Rough approach, in the CSV reading error handling path:

try:
    ...read with utf-8...
except UnicodeDecodeError as e:
    if encoding_was_default:
        raise UnicodeDecodeError(
            e.encoding, e.object, e.start, e.end,
            e.reason + ". Tip: this file may not be UTF-8 encoded. "
            "Try encoding='latin-1' or encoding='cp1252', common with Windows Excel exports."
        ) from e
    raise

This only changes the message text, not behavior, and only fires when encoding wasn't explicitly passed by the user, so it doesn't affect anyone who already specifies an encoding.

Currently the only options are:

1. Manually try common encodings one by one (utf-8, latin-1, cp1252) until one works, usually after searching Stack Overflow to learn this is the fix
2. Use a third-party library like chardet or charset-normalizer to detect the encoding beforehand, which is a heavier dependency for a one-line hint
3. Open the file in a text editor that reports encoding, then pass it explicitly

None of these are discoverable from the error message itself, which is the actual gap this request addresses.

This is intentionally scoped narrower than a full encoding='detect' feature, since I understand that's a bigger design discussion. This is just improving the existing error message text for the common case.

title: Add DataFrame.headtail() to show first and last N rows together
body:
When inspecting a large DataFrame, it's common to want a quick look at both the beginning and the end of the data at the same time — for example, to sanity-check that a sort, concat, or time-series load looks correct from start to finish. Currently this requires calling `df.head()` and `df.tail()` separately and manually comparing the two outputs, which is a bit clunky, especially in notebooks where each call produces a separate output block.

Add a new method, e.g. `DataFrame.headtail(n=5)`, that returns a single DataFrame combining the first `n` and last `n` rows, similar to what `pd.concat([df.head(n), df.tail(n)])` would produce, but as a built-in convenience method. Ideally it would also insert a visual separator (similar to how `describe()` or truncated display uses `...`) to make clear that the middle rows are omitted, rather than implying the rows are contiguous.

Example usage:

```python
df.headtail(5)
```

Possible output:

```
   col1  col2
0     1     a
1     2     b
2     3     c
3     4     d
4     5     e
..  ...   ...
95   96     f
96   97     g
97   98     h
98   99     i
99  100     j
```

- Users can already do `pd.concat([df.head(n), df.tail(n)])`, but this doesn't include a visual separator and requires an extra import/call pattern.
- `pd.set_option('display.max_rows', 10)` combined with printing the full DataFrame gives a similar truncated view, but it changes global display state rather than returning a usable object, and doesn't work well outside of print/repr.

This would mainly be a display/inspection convenience method, similar in spirit to `head()`/`tail()`/`sample()`, useful for quick EDA on large DataFrames in notebooks and scripts.

title: Add optional checkpointing and recovery for long-running apply operations
body:
Long-running Series.apply() and DataFrame.apply() operations can be vulnerable to unexpected process or kernel termination.

Currently, intermediate results are kept in memory until the operation completes. If the Python process terminates unexpectedly, all successfully computed intermediate results may be lost, even if most or all rows have already been processed.

It would be useful to provide an optional checkpointing mechanism that periodically persists completed results during apply() execution.

For example, users could specify a checkpoint file and checkpoint interval. If execution is interrupted, a subsequent run could restore the checkpoint and continue processing only the remaining rows.

This could be particularly useful for expensive per-row operations such as API requests, machine learning inference, LLM calls, network operations, or computationally expensive transformations.

The goal would not be to handle the process crash itself, since pandas cannot execute recovery code after the process has already terminated. Instead, intermediate results would be persisted proactively during normal execution so that they can be recovered afterwards.

result = df[“column”].apply(
expensive_function,
checkpoint=“apply_checkpoint.pkl”,
checkpoint_every=10,
)

for i, value in df["column"].items():
    df.at[i, "result"] = expensive_function(value)

    if i % 10 == 0:
        df.to_pickle("checkpoint.pkl")

So what I do now - is "guess" poetry's venv path in my specific build and hope it won't randomly change later.

title: Clarify "poetry lock" suggestion provided for `poetry self` subcommands
body:
When a lock file is outdated, the provided suggestion is to run `poetry lock`. The same suggestion applies for `poetry self` subcommands - ex `poetry self sync`:

*"pyproject.toml changed significantly since poetry.lock was last generated. Run `poetry lock` to fix the lock file"*

For `poetry self` subcommands however, the fix would be `poetry self lock`:
- `poetry lock` references `pyproject.toml` from the current project/directory. 
- `poetry self lock` references `pyproject.toml` from the Poetry installation directory:
    - macOS - `~/Library/Application\ Support/pypoetry`
    - Linux - `~/.config/pypoetry`
    - Windows - `%APPDATA%\pypoetry`

Assuming the user is likely to be in a different directory, they might see *"Poetry could not find a pyproject.toml file"* or a lock file from an unrelated project gets updated. `poetry lock` updates the expected lock file in this case only if you're in the Poetry installation directory - it does also create a virtualenv and I'm not sure if this may present other unintended consequences.

---

**Proposal**
- An outdated lock file from a regular command continues to suggest `poetry lock`
- An outdated lock file from a `poetry self` subcommand suggests `poetry self lock`

I did not find an existing issue on this, apologies in advance if I missed a duplicate issue!

Could reduce potential confusion/errors for the user

- Running `poetry self lock`
- Running `poetry lock` as suggested, but specifically in the Poetry installation configuration directory
    - macOS - `~/Library/Application\ Support/pypoetry`
    - Linux - `~/.config/pypoetry`
    - Windows - `%APPDATA%\pypoetry`

title: support for Conda-backed virtual environments
body:
Feature Request

Summary:
Allow Poetry to create and manage project environments using Anaconda/Miniconda instead of the built-in venv.

Motivation:
On some Windows systems, installing packages like NumPy or Pandas from source is difficult due to the lack of a C/C++ toolchain. Conda solves this by distributing pre-built binaries.

The current workaround is:
* Manually create a Conda environment.
* Install Poetry into that environment.
* Activate it.
* Run Poetry commands inside.

Problems with this approach:
* Environment setup becomes a manual multi-step process instead of poetry install.
* "poetry run" is no longer usable as intended, since Poetry does not own the environment lifecycle.

Proposed design
===

Add a configuration option in pyproject.toml:

```
[tool.poetry.env]
engine = "conda"                # default remains "venv"
conda-path = "/path/to/conda"   # optional
env-name = "custom-name"        # optional override
```

Behaviour:
* Default naming follows Poetry’s existing environment scheme.
* If engine = "conda", Poetry invokes Conda to create and manage the environment.
* All normal Poetry workflows (poetry install, poetry run, etc.) work seamlessly.

Benefits
* Simplifies setup for Windows where compilers are unavailable.
* Retains full Poetry workflows.
* Supports teams standardising on Conda.

The motivation for this issue is that on some platforms—particularly Windows—users may lack the necessary compiler toolchains required to build scientific Python libraries such as NumPy or Pandas from source. While Conda provides pre-built binary distributions that solve this problem, the current workflow requires manually creating and managing a Conda environment outside of Poetry’s control, installing Poetry inside it, and then running commands within that context. This breaks the simplicity of Poetry’s standard workflow, which is designed around a single command (poetry install) to set up a project environment and poetry run to execute commands in that environment.

By adding support for Conda as an environment backend, Poetry would streamline the setup process for users who rely on Conda, allowing them to keep the same developer experience as those using the default venv. This would ensure that poetry install works consistently across different systems, regardless of compiler availability, and that poetry run can still be used as intended. The improvement is especially important for teams working in mixed environments or organisations standardising on Conda, as it allows Poetry to integrate seamlessly into existing workflows while reducing friction for users who would otherwise have to maintain two separate environment-management steps.

Current workaround steps:
	1.	Use Conda (Anaconda or Miniconda) to manually create a new environment:

conda create -n myenv python=3.11

	2.	Activate the environment:

conda activate myenv

	3.	Install Poetry into this Conda environment:

pip install poetry

	4.	Run poetry install inside the activated Conda environment to install project dependencies.
	5.	To execute commands, activate the Conda environment first, then run poetry run ....

This sequence works but breaks the usual single-step workflow and prevents poetry run from automatically managing activation.

When upgrading poetry to 2.2.0 and beyond, names of dependency groups are now silently normalized: https://github.com/python-poetry/poetry/pull/10387 which can act cause a breaking change.

Because I happened to have the latest poetry,  while the lock in the repo was generated with `2.1.4`, the normalization changed the names of the groups in the lock file. I think it would be a good idea to either:

- return an error when using `--with` option when specified group name does not exist in the lock file

title: Add poetry remove --unused to automatically detect and remove unused dependencies
body:
Poetry currently offers powerful dependency management, but it lacks a built-in way to automatically detect unused dependencies in a project.

I would like to propose a new command:

poetry remove --unused

This command would:

1.Scan the project’s .py files to determine which modules are actually imported

2.Compare those modules against the packages listed in pyproject.toml

3.dentify dependencies that are declared but never used

4.Prompt the user to remove them (or remove automatically with --yes)

Example usage:

poetry remove --unused
poetry remove --unused --yes
poetry remove --unused --json

Example output:

Detected unused dependencies:
  • requests
  • pandas

Remove these packages? (y/N)

This feature benefits users by:

Preventing dependency bloat

Reducing environment size and installation times

Improving security by eliminating unused packages

Making Docker images smaller

Helping maintain long-term projects where dependencies accumulate

Simplifying debugging of conflicts caused by stale dependencies

Unused dependencies are a common issue in Python projects, especially larger codebases.
A built-in solution in Poetry aligns perfectly with its mission of safe, clean dependency management.

There are partial workarounds, but none fully integrated with Poetry:

deptry – detects unused dependencies but does not remove them

pip-autoremove – pip-based; not Poetry-aware

Manual scanning of imports

Manually removing packages one-by-one

None of these provide a Poetry-native, declarative, single-command solution.
A built-in poetry remove --unused solves this cleanly and consistently.

PEP 770 introduces a standardized way for Python packages to include Software Bill‑of‑Materials (SBOM) data inside wheel distributions—specifically within a new .dist-info/sboms/ directory.

title: Does the project consider DataFrame.query() arbitrary code execution to be a security vulnerability?
body:
https://stackoverflow.com/questions/79304226/should-i-manually-patch-the-pandas-dataframe-query-vulnerability-or-wait-for-a

(To clarify, this question was written by another user.)

Hi, I saw [this question on StackOverflow](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/79304226/should-i-manually-patch-the-pandas-dataframe-query-vulnerability-or-wait-for-a), which is about a public CVE, [CVE-2024-9880](https://huntr.com/bounties/a49baae1-4652-4d6c-a179-313c21c41a8d).

The basic premise of the CVE is that if an attacker controls the `expr` argument to DataFrame.query(), then arbitrary code execution can be achieved.

The example given in the CVE is 

<details>

```python
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({'a': [1, 2, 3], 'b': ['error_details', 'confidential_info', 'normal']})

query = '@pd.core.frame.com.builtins.__import__("os").system("""ping google.com #""")'
try:
    engine = "python"
    result = df.query(query,local_dict={},engine="python",).index
except Exception as e:
    print(f'Error: {e}')
```

</details>

However, this is not minimal, and a more minimal construction would be 

```python
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame()

expr = '@pd.compat.os.system("""echo foo""")'
result = df.query(expr, engine='python')
```

(The report also says that `engine='python'` is required, but both `engine='python'` and `engine='numexpr'` worked in my testing.)

My question is about Pandas's security model. What security guarantees does Pandas make about DataFrame.query() with an attacker-controlled `expr`?

My intuition about this is "none, don't do that," but I'm wondering what the Pandas project thinks.

title: best way to extend/subclass pandas.DataFrame
body:
https://stackoverflow.com/questions/79594258/best-way-to-extend-subclass-pandas-dataframe

I've written a [package](https://www.github.com/rwijtvliet/portfolyo) to work with energy-related timeseries. At its center is a class ([`PfLine`](https://portfolyo.readthedocs.io/en/latest/core/pfline.html)) that is essentially a wrapper around pandas.DataFrame, and it implements various methods and properties that are also available on DataFrames - like `.loc`, `.asfreq()`, `.index`, etc.

I am currently in the middle of a rewrite of this package, and think it would be a good idea to have closer integration with pandas. [This page](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/development/extending.html) lays out several possibilities, and I am unsure which route to take - and was hoping to find some sparring here.

Let me describe a bit what I'm trying to accomplish with the `PfLine` class:

  * Behaves like a DataFrame, with specific column names allowed and some data conversion (and validation) on initialisation.

  * Is immutable to avoid data from becoming inconsistent.

  * Has additional methods.

The methods could be directly under `PfLine.method()` or under e.g. `df.pfl.method()`.

What is probably important: a way is needed for the user to specify a (still under development) configuration object (`commodity`) when initialising the PfLine. This object contains information used in coercing the data, e.g. what are the correct units and which timezones are allowed for the index.

title: Poetry lock file hashes differ depending on the platform
body:
Poetry lock file hashes differ depending on the platform

- **Poetry version**: 1.7.0
- **Python version**: 3.8 (also tested in 3.10)
- **OS version and name**: Windows 10 (also on other OS)

Hello everyone,

When using the command ```poetry lock```, the generated hashes differ depending on the OS/Platform. 

Concretely, this means that a lock file generated locally, on a Windows computer, will be different than if it was generated on a Linux CI/CD pipeline. Therefore, it is impossible to use ```poetry install``` on our pipelines as the provided hashes will not work in this environment.

Is there a way to make these hashes platform-agnostic ?

Context : we want to use Poetry to freeze our dependencies versions. The idea here is that the developer generates the lock file, and the CI/CD pipeline will use ```poetry install``` so that the code dependencies will be exactly the same as locally. This allows us to prevent error from transitive dependencies. The problem is that our computers OS is different than the pipeline platform, so we cannot use ````poetry install```, as this will crash due to the hashes not being recognized properly.

Thank you !

# pyproject.toml

This installs fine and allows me to execute binaries such as:

```sh

poetry run pytest .

However, after changing my layout to use `src/` and updating `pyproject.toml` `packages` accordingly, those commands above stop working, raising errors related to missing modules.
